excerpt.title: Validate persistent workflows with transition matrices and full-state sequence tests
excerpt.scope: For persistent event-driven state machines whose evaluator checks exact outputs and complete graph state across ordered operations and restarts. Evidence: compilation succeeded and all 20 public cases passed, but the overall result was [numeric outcome redacted], so public examples and surface checks were insufficient. The specific reason for the six failures is unknown.
steps: Translate the specification into a transition matrix covering each operation, every lifecycle state, actor authorization, boundary value, duplicate action, and missing entity.
For every matrix row, define the exact output, permitted object and relation changes, and all graph elements that must remain unchanged.
Implement validation before mutation so every error path is atomic.
Persist idempotency receipts in the graph, using a canonical fingerprint that excludes transport-only identifiers, and check receipts before domain processing.
Generate tests with fresh identifiers rather than replaying only published examples.
Exercise ordered sequences, including valid transitions followed by every operation against terminal states.
Run replay tests for both identical and conflicting payloads, asserting exact output and zero graph mutation on replay or conflict.
Snapshot the complete logical graph after every event and compare objects, relations, counts, and field values—not only emitted output.
Reload the runtime midway through representative sequences and continue from persisted graph state.
If the official framework is unavailable, build a small deterministic harness around the supplied evaluator or runtime instead of reducing validation to compilation and visible cases.
pitfalls: Treating a perfect public-case result as completion when sealed checks exercise novel entities, ordered transitions, and restart behavior.
Inferring the six failing cases from the scalar score; the available evidence does not identify their inputs or causes.
Testing only returned outputs while overlooking unexpected mutations, missing relations, duplicate receipts, or incorrect persisted state.
Relying on module-local state in workflows that must survive runtime reloads.
Skipping broader validation when a preferred test framework is unavailable.
validation: Compilation or import succeeds.
Published examples pass, but are treated only as a baseline.
Generated unseen-identifier cases cover all transition-matrix rows and numeric boundaries.
Each event emits exactly one completion with the required correlation identifier.
Error paths and terminal-state operations leave the graph unchanged except where the specification explicitly requires a receipt.
Identical operation replay returns the stored output without mutation; conflicting reuse returns the specified conflict without mutation.
Graph snapshots remain equivalent across a cold reload, and subsequent operations produce the same outputs and state transitions.

excerpt.title: Use checkpointed media extraction and persist the deliverable incrementally
excerpt.scope: For tasks that extract structured actions from video or other external media. The only direct evidence here is that the attempt raised before responding, created no artifact, and scored zero; therefore the reusable lesson is a failure-avoidance strategy rather than a demonstrated successful extraction method.
steps: Check that the media URL is reachable and identify the available download, subtitle, frame-extraction, OCR, and audio-transcription tools.
Download the media to a local path and verify that the file exists, is nonempty, and can be decoded.
Inspect subtitles or metadata first, but treat them only as candidate evidence when the required information is visually displayed rather than spoken.
Sample frames across the full duration to determine where player input appears and how it differs visually from game output.
Extract frames around each input event, using tighter time intervals when text changes rapidly.
Transcribe only player-entered commands, preserving their chronological order and original wording.
Normalize each command to one line while avoiding unsupported spelling corrections or inferred commands.
Write the destination artifact early, update it incrementally, and close it cleanly so partial progress survives later tool failures.
If a tool fails, record the failed checkpoint, try an available fallback, and still return a concise status rather than raising without a final response.
pitfalls: Allowing a download, decoding, OCR, or transcription error to terminate the run before producing any response.
Claiming extraction accuracy when no artifact or intermediate evidence exists.
Mixing displayed game output with player-entered commands.
Writing commentary, prompts, timestamps, or blank lines into a command-only deliverable.
validation: Confirm the output file exists at the exact requested path and has nonzero size when commands were observed.
Check that every nonempty line contains exactly one command and no timestamps, prompts, narration, or game responses.
Review the opening, middle, and ending portions of the media to detect missed intervals.
Compare each output line against its source frame and verify chronological ordering.
Report uncertainty or incomplete coverage explicitly instead of presenting an unverified transcript as complete.

excerpt.title: Apply semantic axis defaults at finalization, then honor explicit overrides
excerpt.scope: For plotting systems where a semantic scale requires categorical-style presentation, apply axis-dependent defaults during figure finalization, when locators and ticks are available, and then apply explicit user configuration last. The passing grader and manual checks support this ordering for nominal bounds, grid suppression, and y-axis inversion.
steps: Identify the resolved semantic scale for each physical axis, including scales inferred from data.
During figure finalization, detect axes whose resolved scale requires categorical presentation.
Derive default view bounds from the finalized major tick positions or count so the view extends half a category beyond the outer ticks.
Disable the major grid on that categorical-style axis.
For a vertical categorical-style axis, invert it only when it is not already inverted.
After applying semantic defaults, apply explicit user limits so user configuration takes precedence.
Exercise both inferred and explicitly declared scales on horizontal and vertical axes.
pitfalls: Applying categorical defaults before tick locations are finalized can produce incorrect bounds.
Reapplying axis inversion without checking current state can accidentally restore the original orientation.
Scale-derived defaults must not overwrite explicit user limits.
A dependency compatibility error in the broader suite should be reported separately rather than treated as a product-code regression.
validation: Verify a nominal horizontal axis extends half a unit beyond its first and last category ticks.
Verify a nominal vertical axis has the corresponding reversed bounds and reports as inverted.
Verify grid lines are hidden for both inferred and explicitly declared nominal scales.
Verify explicit user limits override semantic defaults.
Run focused tests before the full suite and distinguish code failures from dependency or environment incompatibilities.
Run the repository's whitespace or diff-integrity check.

excerpt.title: Normalize fractional counts before integer-only downstream APIs
excerpt.scope: Applies when an API accepts a fractional size or count but a downstream component requires an integer count. Normalize the value once at the boundary between public parameter semantics and downstream construction, while preserving rounding and minimum-bound rules. This procedure is supported by a successful smoke test, a 40-test focused suite, and the passing grader receipt.
steps: Trace the parameter from public input through validation and arithmetic to the first downstream consumer with stricter type requirements.
Identify the documented conversion semantics for fractional values, including rounding behavior and minimum or maximum bounds.
After fraction-to-count arithmetic and bound enforcement, explicitly convert the result to the required integer type.
Keep the normalized value for all subsequent uses so downstream components receive consistent values.
Limit the patch to the normalization boundary unless evidence shows other call paths require changes.
pitfalls: Do not pass a numerically integral float to APIs that require an integer type; value validity does not imply type validity.
Do not cast before applying the intended rounding rule, because truncation may change parameter semantics.
Preserve documented lower bounds after converting fractions to absolute counts.
validation: Reproduce the failing path with a fractional input and verify the full operation completes.
Test a fraction whose product is non-integral to exercise the rounding rule.
Test small inputs to verify the minimum count remains enforced.
Run the focused component test suite and a repository diff/style check.
Confirm that existing integer-valued inputs retain their prior behavior.

excerpt.title: Split composite declarations at the component with the stable boundary
excerpt.scope: Applies when parsing a field whose final whitespace-delimited token is an identifier and whose preceding expression may contain internal whitespace, such as parameter declarations, annotations, or compact metadata syntax. The successful focused test and evaluator receipt support this procedure for that grammar; they do not establish that right-splitting is appropriate when names may contain whitespace or trailing modifiers.
steps: Write down the field grammar and identify which component has the stronger boundary invariant.
If the name is defined as the final whitespace-delimited token while the preceding expression may contain spaces, split once from the right rather than from the left.
Preserve the existing malformed-input behavior, including the no-delimiter case, unless the task explicitly changes it.
Add a regression input containing whitespace inside the leading expression so the original tokenization error is exercised.
Assert the complete structured result: extracted name, complete expression, punctuation, content, and semantic reference nodes where applicable.
Run the narrowest relevant test module first, then perform repository formatting or diff checks.
pitfalls: Splitting from the left assumes the type is a single token and can silently misidentify part of a spaced type expression as the parameter name.
Testing only rendered text may miss malformed links or node boundaries in structured documentation output.
After inserting a regression fixture into an ordered structure, update and verify assertions for all shifted siblings.
validation: The focused documentation-domain test suite passed all 45 tests after the change.
The regression covered a composite datatype containing a comma followed by whitespace.
The assertion checked the rendered node structure, including the parameter name, datatype components, references, punctuation, and description.
The repository diff whitespace check passed.
The official evaluator returned a passing score.

excerpt.title: Validate persistent workflows with model-based sequence and graph-state tests
excerpt.scope: For persistent event-driven workflows evaluated through unseen ordered sequences. The evidence shows that compilation and all 20 public checks passed, while the overall evaluator score was [numeric outcome redacted] and did not pass. This supports a changed validation strategy: derive a transition model from the specification and test outputs plus complete persisted state after every event. The evidence does not identify which sealed cases failed, so no specific implementation defect should be asserted.
steps: Translate the specification into a state-transition table covering each operation, precondition, success mutation, error output, and required no-mutation behavior.

List boundary partitions independently of visible examples, including blank identifiers, duplicate entities, threshold values, role combinations, requester/actor identity, duplicate actions, and terminal states.
Define an oracle snapshot containing the exact emitted event, all logical objects, all relations, and relevant mutation counts after every input.
Generate short ordered sequences that cover each transition and pairwise interaction, rather than testing operations only in isolation.
For every error path, compare the post-event graph with the pre-event graph and allow only explicitly required bookkeeping mutations.
Test idempotency in three modes: first use, identical replay, and conflicting replay; verify exact output and graph stability.
Insert a cold runtime reload midway through representative sequences, then repeat replay, authorization, and transition checks against persisted state.
Exercise threshold and terminal-state boundaries explicitly, including values immediately below and at each threshold.
Verify deterministic canonicalization and fingerprinting with equivalent and distinct payloads.
Run visible tests and compilation only as preliminary gates; require the model-based sequence suite to pass before considering the implementation complete.
pitfalls: Treating full visible-example coverage as evidence that generalized stateful behavior is correct.
Testing only returned outputs while omitting the complete graph state, relations, and mutation count.
Checking operations individually but not error precedence, replay behavior, terminal-state transitions, or ordered sequences.
Using compilation as a behavioral correctness signal.
Assuming restart persistence without recreating the runtime and continuing the same sequence.
validation: The supplied public runner completed [numeric outcome redacted] successfully.
The implementation compiled successfully.
The final evaluator score was [numeric outcome redacted] and marked failed, demonstrating that those two gates were insufficient.

excerpt.title: Make reset operations lifecycle-aware instead of reinitializing all configuration
excerpt.scope: Applies when a clear or reset operation causes UI, plotting, or component appearance to regress because persistent configuration and transient runtime state are stored together. The successful evidence supports selectively preserving appearance settings while resetting only state with an explicit reset contract.
steps: Reproduce the defect both in the composed scenario, such as linked or shared components, and on a standalone component to separate integration symptoms from the core reset bug.
Trace the clear path to every helper that recreates, empties, or repopulates configuration dictionaries and cached defaults.
Classify each field by lifecycle: persistent user or layout configuration, transient generated state, or configuration-derived state that must be recomputed.
Replace broad dictionary reinitialization with targeted updates: retain persistent fields, discard transient objects, and recompute only fields whose contract requires current global defaults.
Ensure newly created child objects consume the preserved configuration after the reset.
Keep the patch localized unless tests demonstrate that the lifecycle classification must change elsewhere.
pitfalls: Do not treat clear or reset as necessarily meaning that every configuration field should return to a constructor default.
Reinitializing cached defaults can discard externally established state such as shared-layout visibility or style settings.
Preserving every field indiscriminately can retain transient state that is explicitly expected to follow current configuration defaults.
validation: Exercise repeated clear-and-reuse cycles, not only the first reset.
Verify both the shared or linked layout and a standalone instance.
Assert persistent visibility and appearance settings remain unchanged after clearing.
Assert intentionally reset state follows current configuration defaults.
Run focused tests around clearing, ticks, sharing, and configuration, then run a diff or formatting check.
[external outcome redacted].

excerpt.title: Validate canonical layout positioning across engine and coordinate-system branches
excerpt.scope: Applies to layout and geometry bugs where spacing parameters are ignored and placement differs by layout engine or nesting level. The attempt evidenced that using the canonical positioning API can expose spacing and that one spanning test passed, but [external outcome redacted].
steps: Identify the canonical geometry API that already incorporates spacing, ratios, margins, and spans; prefer it over manually recomputing normalized bounds.
Enumerate behavior branches before editing: no layout engine, each supported layout engine, zero and nonzero spacing, top-level and nested containers, and single-cell versus spanning placements.
Determine explicitly which component owns spacing in each branch; do not infer ownership solely from whether an engine object exists.
Express every returned bounding box in a documented coordinate system, then perform an explicit transform into the immediate parent's coordinates.
Preserve mutable geometry-object semantics if callers retain references: update existing bounds in place where required instead of replacing objects indiscriminately.
Add focused assertions for both dimensions: positive spacing must create a measurable gap, while zero spacing must align adjacent boundaries within tolerance.
Add regression coverage for nested containers, spans, unequal ratios, repeated draws or resizes, and all relevant layout-engine modes.

Run the focused tests plus the surrounding figure/layout test modules; if broader evaluation fails, reconsider branch selection and coordinate ownership rather than claiming the canonical-position substitution is sufficient.
pitfalls: Treating one existing regression test and a clean diff as evidence that a behavioral fix is complete.
Using a broad condition such as layout-engine presence as a proxy for which component owns spacing without testing every engine state.
Changing coordinate systems without separately checking top-level, nested, spanning, and redraw behavior.
Preserving historical behavior through an inferred special case rather than confirming the owning layout contract.
validation: Compare adjacent bounding-box edges numerically for zero and positive horizontal and vertical spacing.
Verify placements under no engine and every supported engine instead of testing only the default mode.
Check nested bounds after transforming through each immediate parent coordinate system.
Exercise unequal width and height ratios and multi-row or multi-column spans.
Trigger redraw and resize paths to detect stale or incorrectly replaced geometry.
Run nearby layout regression suites in addition to the originally cited spanning test and formatting checks.

excerpt.title: Preserve SQLite WAL evidence before opening the database
excerpt.scope: Applies to forensic recovery or diagnosis of SQLite databases with WAL or journal sidecars, especially when merely opening the database may mutate the evidence. The failed attempt evidences that the WAL disappeared after SQLite access and that base-only extraction was insufficient; it does not establish why the WAL vanished or that its missing records were intrinsically unrecoverable.
steps: Before invoking SQLite or any application that may open the database, list and record metadata for the database, WAL, shared-memory, journal, and related files.
Stop database writers if permitted, then make byte-for-byte copies of the database and every sidecar file into a separate working directory.
Mark the evidence copies read-only and record cryptographic hashes and sizes.
Perform all SQLite access and repair experiments on disposable duplicates of the preserved copies, never on the originals.
Inspect the WAL structurally or at the byte level before trying operations that may checkpoint or remove it.
Try candidate repairs one at a time on fresh duplicates, retaining hashes and logs so each mutation is attributable.
Extract records from a successfully reconstructed copy, sort and serialize them in the required output format.
If reconstruction fails, return to untouched copies and change strategy rather than substituting base-only data for explicitly required WAL content.
pitfalls: Opening the database through SQLite before preserving its sidecar files can trigger recovery, checkpointing, or cleanup that deletes or changes the WAL.
A normal filesystem copy may be inconsistent if another process is writing; stop writers or use a snapshot mechanism first.
Recovering only base-table rows does not satisfy a task that requires WAL-only changes.
Do not claim unrecoverable data values unless preservation and forensic inspection were attempted on immutable copies.
validation: Confirm the preserved WAL exists and its hash remains unchanged after every experiment.
Verify experiments operate only on disposable copies by comparing paths and hashes.
Check recovered row count and required identifiers against the task's stated totals.
Validate the output syntax, schema, ordering, and values before submission.
Treat a base-only result as failure when the requirement explicitly includes uncheckpointed WAL records.

excerpt.title: Reversibly encode foreign identifiers before constructing host-language AST names
excerpt.scope: Applies when a custom expression language is compiled through another language's AST or evaluator and its identifiers have a broader grammar than host-language identifiers. The evidence supports reversible encoding at the AST boundary: the focused suite passed, manual round trips covered constants, keywords, numeric-looking names, punctuation, and Unicode, and [external outcome redacted].
steps: Identify every source-language token that is embedded as a host-language identifier.
Define a deterministic, injective encoding whose output always satisfies the host AST's identifier rules and cannot equal reserved constants or keywords.
Encode identifiers immediately before constructing host AST name nodes.
Decode names only at the adapter boundary immediately before invoking the source-language matcher or resolver.
Keep operators and literal AST nodes separate from encoded user identifiers.
Add explicit malformed-input handling or assertions so unexpected evaluator lookups fail locally.
Test both semantic matching and the invariant decode(encode(value)) == value across representative edge classes.
pitfalls: Do not insert user-controlled tokens directly into a host-language AST; source-language-valid names may be reserved, syntactically invalid, or rejected by compiler invariants.
Avoid non-injective sanitization such as replacing punctuation with underscores, because distinct inputs can collide.
Ensure generated names are valid in every supported runtime, not merely accepted by the parser on one version.
Decode only names produced by the encoder, and reject malformed encoded keys rather than silently misrouting them.
validation: Run the focused parser and expression test suite.
Round-trip empty or boundary cases plus ordinary names, reserved constants, keywords, numeric-looking names, punctuation, and Unicode.
Verify distinct source identifiers produce distinct encoded names.
Compile and evaluate expressions containing each edge class, confirming the matcher receives the exact original identifier.
Run formatting or whitespace checks such as a diff consistency check.
Where available, test on the affected runtime versions or debug builds because compiler assertions may not appear in release builds.

excerpt.title: Normalize fractional count parameters before integer-only dependencies
excerpt.scope: Use when an API accepts either an absolute integer count or a fractional proportion, but downstream components require a strict integer. Normalize the proportion once its reference population is known, preserve documented lower bounds and rounding semantics, and apply the same conversion in every path that interprets the parameter.
steps: Find every location that validates, derives, forwards, or reuses the dual-form count parameter.
After the population size is available, convert fractional input into an absolute count using the repository's specified rounding rule.
Enforce any minimum or maximum bound as part of the conversion.
Explicitly cast the normalized result to an integer before passing it to strict downstream constructors or algorithms.
Apply equivalent normalization in fitting, extraction, prediction, and helper paths that share the parameter's meaning.
Add a regression test using a fractional value that previously reached an integer-only dependency.
Run the focused module tests and a repository formatting or diff-integrity check.
pitfalls: Do not assume arithmetic on an integer count and a fractional parameter produces an integer acceptable to downstream APIs.
Do not normalize a shared parameter in only one code path when fitting and post-processing use the same semantics.
A smoke test that checks output shape proves successful execution, but not the exact rounding behavior at boundary values.
validation: Evidence showed that explicitly rounding and casting the derived count in both relevant OPTICS paths passed all 41 focused tests.
The regression fit with a fractional parameter completed and produced an ordering with the expected sample-count shape.
The patch passed the official evaluator and `git diff --check`.
For stronger semantic coverage in future work, test values around rounding thresholds and lower-bound enforcement, not only successful execution.

excerpt.title: Separate public validation from trusted internal computation
excerpt.scope: Applies when a fit or training routine validates input, stores metadata such as feature names, and then calls a public inference or scoring method on an already transformed or validated representation. Revalidation can produce false metadata warnings or redundant work. The evidenced approach passed the targeted test suite and official evaluation.
steps: Trace the warning to any public prediction, transformation, or scoring method called internally during fitting.
Determine whether fit has already validated the exact data and whether the internal computation requires any additional checks.
Extract the post-validation computation into a private helper whose contract requires already validated input.
Keep validation in the public method, then delegate from it to the private helper.
Call the private helper only from internal paths that can guarantee its preconditions.
Add a regression test using metadata-bearing input and the option that activates the problematic internal path.
Configure the test to turn the specific unexpected warning category into an error.
pitfalls: Do not bypass validation for public methods or caller-provided data.
Do not suppress the warning globally; remove the redundant operation that causes it.
A warning-free regression alone does not prove that computed results remain unchanged.
validation: Run the focused module test suite; the evidenced change passed 22 tests.
Verify the regression test fails on the warning by treating the relevant warning category as an error.
Check that the public API still validates external input before delegating.
Where feasible, compare outputs before and after refactoring to confirm the private path preserves computation.
Run repository formatting or whitespace checks; the evidenced change passed diff checking.

excerpt.title: Validate gcov builds at compile, link, discovery, and runtime layers
excerpt.scope: Use this procedure when building a vendored C or C++ command-line application with gcov coverage and exposing it through PATH. The successful evidence supports layered verification: confirm executable discovery and version, inspect the final binary for coverage runtime linkage, execute it, and verify that runtime coverage data appears alongside matching compile-time metadata.
steps: Extract and build the required vendored source snapshot without network access.
Apply gcov-compatible coverage options during both compilation and linking, typically through the build system's compiler and linker flag variables.
Retain the generated .gcno metadata files and install or link the resulting executable into a directory already present in PATH.
Run the installed executable at least once with a simple command so instrumented code executes and coverage data can be written.
Locate the resulting .gcda files and confirm that corresponding .gcno files from the same build remain available.
pitfalls: Checking only the reported version or executable location does not prove coverage instrumentation is active.
Compiler flags may be lost during configure or link stages; verify the final binary and runtime artifacts.
Running from an unwritable directory or with incompatible coverage paths can prevent .gcda creation.
Fetching upstream sources when a vendored snapshot is required harms reproducibility and may violate task constraints.
validation: Resolve the executable through PATH and verify that it runs.
Check the executable's version to confirm the intended build is being invoked.
Inspect the final binary for a gcov runtime marker such as __gcov_init.
Execute a representative command and verify that one or more .gcda files are created.
Confirm matching .gcno files are retained for later coverage analysis.

excerpt.title: Parse trailing identifiers from the right when leading expressions may contain whitespace
excerpt.scope: Applicable when parsing declarations composed of a potentially whitespace-containing expression followed by a final identifier, especially documentation fields, annotations, signatures, and lightweight DSLs.
steps: Reproduce the defect with an input whose leading expression contains internal whitespace.
Identify the grammar boundary: if the trailing identifier is the stable component, split once from the right rather than assuming the second whitespace token is the identifier.
Preserve the complete leading substring as the expression and use only the final token as the name.
Add an end-to-end regression fixture that passes the problematic declaration through the normal rendering or transformation pipeline.
Assert the resulting name and expression separately and within the relevant output context.
Run the focused output suite, then the broader affected suite, and perform repository formatting or diff checks.
pitfalls: Do not split a structured declaration at the first internal whitespace when its leading expression may itself contain spaces.
Do not validate only parser internals when the reported defect concerns rendered output.
Avoid assertions so broad that a correct parameter name could be paired with an incorrect or truncated type elsewhere in the document.
validation: [external outcome redacted].
A broader HTML build suite passed 216 tests before the final focused assertion was added.
The regression fixture checked that the final token became the parameter name and the complete leading expression remained the type.

excerpt.title: Validate gcov builds from compilation through runtime data generation
excerpt.scope: Use this procedure when building a vendored C or C++ command-line program with GCC gcov coverage and exposing the resulting executable through PATH. The passing attempt evidences that combining compile-time and link-time coverage flags, installing the intended binary, executing it, and checking for generated coverage data is an effective end-to-end workflow.
steps: Build from the required local source snapshot rather than substituting a network-fetched or system-provided source.
Use GCC-compatible coverage instrumentation in the compile flags, such as -O0 -g --coverage, to preserve useful coverage mapping and debugging information.
Add --coverage to the linker flags as well so the final executable links the gcov runtime.
Install or link the resulting executable into a directory already present in PATH.
Resolve the command with command -v and confirm that it points to the newly installed executable.
Run a lightweight command against the installed executable to exercise the instrumented program and flush runtime coverage data.
Inspect the build output directories for newly generated .gcda files.
pitfalls: Setting coverage flags only during compilation may omit instrumentation at link time; apply coverage flags to both CFLAGS and LDFLAGS.
Checking only the program version or PATH location does not prove that coverage instrumentation works.
A successful build alone is insufficient because .gcda files are generally created only after the instrumented executable runs.
Using a pre-existing system binary can accidentally validate the wrong build; verify the resolved executable path.
validation: Run command -v <program> and verify the resolved path is the intended installation.
Run <program> --version or another smoke test to confirm that the installed executable starts successfully.
Inspect the executable for __gcov symbols as supporting evidence that instrumentation was linked.
Execute the program, then locate at least one .gcda file associated with its object files; this demonstrates that runtime coverage collection is functioning.
Record the reported program version when the task targets a specific source snapshot or release.

excerpt.title: Reversibly encode domain identifiers before host-AST compilation
excerpt.scope: Use when a custom expression language is translated into another language's AST and its identifiers are valid in the domain but reserved or otherwise unsafe for the host compiler. The evidence supports reversible identifier encoding before AST compilation and decoding at matcher lookup: focused and neighboring tests passed, and the submitted change received a passing grader score.
steps: Identify the boundary where domain-language identifiers become host AST name nodes.
Define a uniform, reversible, collision-free encoding that maps every domain identifier to a compiler-safe host name.
Encode identifiers when constructing the AST rather than special-casing only the reported reserved words.
Decode names at the lookup or callback boundary so downstream matching continues to receive the original domain identifier.
Keep operators, grouping, and other expression semantics unchanged.
Run focused expression-compilation tests, then adjacent integration tests, and perform a patch-format check.
pitfalls: Passing domain identifiers directly into a host-language AST can violate compiler invariants even when the domain grammar accepts them.
Encoding only currently known reserved words can miss other host-language restrictions; applying one reversible encoding to every identifier is more robust.
Decoding at the wrong boundary can change matcher semantics or expose encoded names to application callbacks.
A non-bijective encoding can cause distinct domain identifiers to collide.
validation: Compile expressions containing host-reserved names and confirm compilation completes without an assertion or crash.
Verify the matcher receives the exact original identifier after decoding.
Test ordinary identifiers alongside reserved identifiers to detect semantic regressions.
Test multiple identifiers and boolean operators to ensure lookup and expression behavior remain intact.
Run both the focused expression suite and related marker or integration suites.
The supplied attempt evidenced 82 focused tests passing, 172 related tests passing with 1 expected failure, a clean diff check, and a passing external grader receipt.

excerpt.title: Validate persistent workflows with transition matrices and restartable sequence tests
excerpt.scope: Use this method for persistent event-driven workflows, graph behaviors, state machines, and APIs whose correctness depends on operation ordering, idempotency, exact outputs, mutation atomicity, and restart durability. The evidence shows that compilation and all 20 public checks passed while the overall evaluation still failed at [numeric outcome redacted]; it does not identify which sealed cases failed.
steps: Translate the specification into a transition table with one row per operation and columns for preconditions, validation precedence, exact output, object changes, relation changes, and forbidden partial mutations.
Enumerate each operation across every reachable entity state, including missing, initial, intermediate, and terminal states.
Create ordered sequence tests that revisit the same entities rather than testing each operation only in isolation.
For every rejection path, snapshot the logical graph before execution and assert that objects and relations are unchanged afterward.
Test idempotency as a three-part sequence: first execution, same identifier with identical domain payload, and same identifier with a changed domain payload.
Repeat the replay and conflict checks after recreating the runtime from persisted graph state.
Compare the complete logical graph and the exact emitted payload after every event, including event count and correlation identifier.
Add boundary cases for blanks, duplicates, malformed collections, missing endpoints, invalid transitions, and competing validation failures.
Use public examples as contract fixtures, then add generated entities and longer sequences so validation does not depend on memorized identifiers.
pitfalls: Treating visible-example success as evidence that unseen state transitions are correct.
Checking only returned values while overlooking unintended object or relation mutations.
Testing operations independently instead of as ordered sequences over persistent state.
Assuming syntax compilation validates runtime graph semantics.
Claiming a specific hidden failure cause when only an aggregate score is available.
validation: Run syntax or import checks, but treat them only as structural validation.
Require all visible fixtures to pass unchanged.
Exercise every transition-table row with fresh, non-fixture identifiers.
Assert exactly one completion event per request and exact payload equality.
Assert full object and relation snapshots after every successful and rejected event.
Cold-reload midway through representative sequences and confirm equivalent subsequent behavior.
Verify repeated identical requests do not mutate state and conflicting reuse also leaves state unchanged.

excerpt.title: Establish a valid baseline artifact before correctness-preserving optimization
excerpt.scope: Use this procedure for repository tasks that require optimizing a configuration or model while preserving behavior. The only direct evidence here is that the attempt raised before responding, produced no owned artifact, and received a failing score; therefore the lesson is procedural rather than evidence that any particular MuJoCo tuning technique works.
steps: Inspect the reference input, evaluation script, required output path, runtime target, and correctness tolerance before editing.
Run the evaluator on the unchanged reference and record baseline runtime, final-state output, and numerical validity.
Immediately create the required output as an unchanged copy of the reference, leaving the reference untouched.
Verify that the copied output loads and completes the evaluator; this establishes a valid fallback artifact before optimization.
Change one performance-related setting at a time, avoiding semantic or physical-property changes unless equivalence has been demonstrated.
After every change, measure runtime and compare the complete required state against the baseline using the stated tolerance.
Reject and revert any candidate that produces NaN or Inf, fails to load, changes required state beyond tolerance, or lacks a repeatable speed improvement.
Keep the fastest correctness-passing candidate at the required output path.
Before finishing, rerun the evaluation from a clean process and confirm both artifact existence and compliance with the runtime threshold.
pitfalls: Beginning optimization before creating a valid output artifact can leave nothing for the evaluator to test.
Treating an unmeasured optimization as successful despite missing benchmark and correctness evidence.
Changing physical or semantic properties when the task requires state-equivalent execution.
Overwriting the reference input instead of preserving a reproducible baseline.
Reporting success after an exception or before checking that required files exist.
validation: Confirm the reference input remains byte-for-byte unchanged.
Confirm the required output file exists, parses, and runs to completion.
Compare the full required final state to the recorded reference with the specified absolute tolerance.
Check all compared values for NaN and Inf.
Measure the same simulation duration and workload for baseline and candidate.
Repeat timing enough to detect unstable or incidental gains.
Accept the candidate only when correctness and runtime requirements pass in the same final run.

excerpt.title: Validate directory-standard migrations with a complete environment precedence matrix
excerpt.scope: Use this method when migrating application state, cache, or configuration paths to an environment-controlled directory standard. The evidence shows that updating precedence, defaults, documentation, and focused tests was not sufficient for acceptance. The exact failure cause is unknown; edge-case environment semantics and import-time state are diagnostic hypotheses, not established grader findings.
steps: Write an explicit precedence table before editing code, covering legacy overrides, the new standard variable, platform defaults, and last-resort fallbacks.

excerpt.title: Validate push-to-deploy systems through the full Git-to-HTTP path

excerpt.title: Inspect lazy-array metadata without crossing a materialization boundary

Run formatting or diff hygiene checks after the test suites.
Evidence for this procedure includes passing focused tests, 1405 passing dataset tests, and a passing official evaluator receipt.

Claiming a specific hidden defect from the scalar score alone; the failed cases and causes were not exposed.

excerpt.title: Front-load feasibility and checkpoint artifacts in video-to-command extraction
excerpt.scope: Applies to tasks that require extracting user-entered commands or other structured events from a video and writing them to a precisely formatted file. Choose a primary extraction route and a fallback, such as frame-based OCR followed by manual review.
Create the required output file early so progress survives later tool failures.

Test predicates that become false and predicates that remain undecidable.
Test domains with and without dependency on the replaced parameter.

Compare ordinary, simultaneous, and structural replacement behavior only where their documented semantics should agree.
Run repository-wide or subsystem-wide tests because the observed targeted run passed while the official grader did not.

excerpt.scope: Applies to repository tasks that require producing a tuned configuration or model under simultaneous performance and exact-correctness constraints. Record baseline runtime, correctness results, and artifact validity.

Overwriting the reference artifact instead of creating a separate candidate.

Check every compared value for NaN and Inf.

Run the supplied evaluator from a fresh process against the final artifact.

steps: Trace the complete metadata flow from the source field through derived-field parameter APIs, migration state, schema alteration, and SQL rendering.
Identify the framework's canonical metadata dictionary or delegation mechanism instead of handling only the visible failing attribute in isolation.
Search existing tests for analogous inherited properties, related-field behavior, and backend-specific schema assertions.
Add a focused regression test that defines a source field with nondefault metadata and verifies that each derived column receives matching metadata.
Cover both initial table creation and field-alteration migrations, because they may use different schema-editor paths.
Exercise representative relationship forms, nullability settings, and custom or wrapped field types when they share the affected abstraction.
Assert structured field or schema parameters where possible, then also assert generated SQL on a backend where the metadata affects constraint compatibility.
Run the focused regression first, followed by the relevant model-field and schema suites and repository formatting checks.
If broad suites pass but the focused case or external evaluation fails, inspect missing execution paths and test coverage rather than presenting the broad pass as confirmation.

validation: Evidence: the generated SQLite column included the referenced key's collation.
Evidence: 430 model-field tests and 179 schema tests passed, with skips.
Evidence: the diff formatting check passed.
Counterevidence: [external outcome redacted].

excerpt.title: Validate push-to-deploy as one complete Git-to-HTTP pipeline
excerpt.scope: Applies to simple push-to-deploy systems where a bare Git repository receives pushes, a server-side hook publishes one designated branch into a web root, and a static HTTP service exposes the result. The successful receipt supports this end-to-end procedure, but does not establish production-grade security, concurrency, rollback, or availability.
steps: Create a bare repository at the SSH-visible path expected by clients.
Create a separate deployment directory that the Git hook can write and the web service can read.
Install a post-receive hook that reads all ref updates and acts only when the designated deployment branch is updated.

For that branch, export the pushed commit into the deployment directory using the bare repository as the Git directory and the web root as the work tree; force replacement when deployment semantics require the tree to exactly match the branch.
Configure the HTTP server to use the deployment directory as its document root and listen on the requested port and required address families.
Validate the server configuration before starting or reloading services.
Run a complete client workflow: clone through the intended transport, commit a uniquely identifiable file, push the deployment branch, and fetch that exact file over HTTP.
pitfalls: Deploying every received ref can publish unintended branches; explicitly gate the hook on the production ref.
A hook checkout may fail because of ownership, permissions, an invalid work tree, or missing force/update handling.
Testing only Git or only HTTP can miss failures at the deployment boundary.
Binding only one address family may make a service unreachable through hostnames that resolve differently.
validation: Confirm the bare repository accepts a clone and push through the same SSH-style path clients will use.
Confirm the hook is executable and a push updates the deployment tree.
Check that non-deployment refs do not alter published content.
Run the HTTP server's configuration validation command.
Fetch the pushed file through the requested hostname and port and compare its body exactly with the committed content.
Where relevant, test both IPv4 and IPv6 listeners.

excerpt.title: Validate push-to-web deployment as one end-to-end pipeline
excerpt.scope: Use this procedure when a push to a bare Git repository must automatically publish static content through a persistent web service. The successful end-to-end result supports the general method of combining a post-receive deployment hook, a separate document root, service persistence, and client-visible validation.
steps: Create a bare repository at the clone/push path expected by clients.
Create a dedicated document root owned or writable by the deployment identity.
Install an executable post-receive hook that reads all ref updates and deploys only the intended branch.
Export the selected commit from the bare repository into the document root, replacing or synchronizing stale files as required.
Configure the HTTP server to bind to the required port and serve the dedicated document root.
Register the server with the host's service manager so it starts persistently and restarts according to policy.
Start or reload the service after installing its configuration.
Exercise the complete workflow from clone through push, then request the deployed file over HTTP.
pitfalls: Do not treat creation of configuration files as proof that deployment or serving works.
A hook that deploys only one branch must explicitly reject or ignore other ref updates.
Ensure the hook is executable and that repository, deployment directory, and service permissions are compatible.
Avoid serving directly from a mutable Git working tree when a separate deployment directory is available.
validation: Clone the repository using the same transport and path clients will use.
Commit and push a uniquely identifiable test file to the deployment branch.
Confirm the hook exits successfully and the file appears in the document root with exact content.
Request the file from the configured HTTP host and port and compare the response body exactly.
Verify the service is active under the service manager and remains available after a service restart.
Delete or rename a tracked file in a later commit and verify the deployed tree handles stale content according to the chosen policy.

excerpt.title: Validate authentication fixes at the actual protocol boundary
excerpt.scope: Use this diagnostic method for authentication failures at protocol boundaries, especially HTTPS requests through an authenticated proxy. The evidence supports wire-level reproduction and clean rollback as sound investigation practices; it does not establish a working fix or identify the exact component that must change.
steps: Build a minimal local endpoint that emulates the relevant intermediary and records the initial protocol exchange.
Reproduce the failure with the smallest client request and confirm whether authentication data appears on the intermediary-facing message, such as CONNECT.
Trace configuration and credentials from the public API through each adapter and dependency boundary to the component that constructs that message.
Instrument or inspect the exact outgoing bytes rather than inferring behavior from final status codes.
Apply one narrowly scoped candidate change at the layer responsible for constructing the intermediary-facing request.
Repeat the local reproduction and reject the change if the required authentication data still does not reach that request.
If standard fixtures are unusable, create an independent focused regression test that avoids the broken fixture while preserving the protocol behavior.
Run focused tests and relevant broader tests; if verification remains impossible or fails, restore the workspace and report the blocker rather than submitting speculative code.
pitfalls: Treating credentials attached to the tunneled HTTP request as equivalent to credentials on the proxy CONNECT request.
Claiming a candidate fix works when wire-level reproduction still shows the required header is absent.
Relying exclusively on a repository test fixture that is broken or recursively dependent.
Retaining speculative changes after validation is blocked or fails.
validation: Assert that the intermediary-facing request contains the expected authentication field before tunneling begins.
Assert that valid credentials change the local reproduction from authentication rejection to successful tunnel establishment.
Include a negative case with missing or invalid credentials to prove the test detects the original failure.
Confirm no credentials are unintentionally forwarded to the destination server.
Check that the final diff contains only changes exercised by passing validation.

excerpt.title: Validate durable graph behaviors with transition matrices and state snapshots
excerpt.scope: For durable event-driven state machines evaluated on unseen entity values and ordered sequences, convert prose requirements into a transition-and-invariant test matrix. The evidence shows that compilation and all 20 visible cases passed, while the overall evaluation scored 38 and failed; therefore visible examples were insufficient validation. The exact defects are not evidenced.
steps: List each operation with its valid preconditions, invalid preconditions, exact output, state mutations, and forbidden mutations.
Model lifecycle fields as an explicit transition table, including repeated operations and invalid transitions from every reachable state.
Define graph invariants separately from output rules, including uniqueness, endpoint existence, relation cardinality, monotonic fields, and allowed object and relation types.
Generate tests with fresh identifiers rather than copying visible fixtures.
Exercise ordered sequences that combine operations, including success followed by error, error followed by success, and repeated transitions.
For every first-seen idempotency key, snapshot output and graph state; verify identical replay returns the stored output with no mutation.
Reuse each idempotency key with a changed domain payload and verify conflict output plus byte-for-byte equivalent logical graph state.
Reload the runtime between operations and rerun replay and continuation checks using only persisted graph data.
After every event, compare the exact emitted-event count, correlation identifier, output structure, objects, relations, and absence of extra graph types.
When the normal test framework is unavailable, create a small deterministic harness that invokes the behavior and performs sequence, snapshot, and reload assertions.
pitfalls: Treating a perfect visible-case score and successful compilation as evidence of full behavioral correctness.
Implementing operations independently without testing ordered sequences, replay, conflict, and restart behavior.
Inferring the specific sealed-test failures from a scalar score; the receipt identifies no failing cases.
Checking event outputs while neglecting exact graph state and absence of partial mutations after errors.
validation: Compilation or import succeeds.
Visible examples pass with exact outputs.
Generated unseen identifiers pass the same rules.
Each lifecycle transition and invalid transition is covered.
Every error path leaves the logical graph unchanged unless mutation is explicitly required.
Replay and operation-id conflict checks preserve graph state.
Cold reload preserves receipts and permits correct sequence continuation.
Exactly one completion event is emitted per request.
Full object and relation snapshots match after every event.

excerpt.title: Validate environment-derived storage changes with a precedence and isolation matrix
excerpt.scope: Use when changing filesystem locations derived from environment variables, especially XDG-style defaults and legacy overrides. The evidence supports checking override precedence, recursive parent creation, documentation, and focused tests, but the zero grader score shows that this particular validation was insufficient; the exact failure cause is not evidenced.
steps: Inventory every read, write, cleanup, migration, help-text, and test reference to the old location before editing.
Define an explicit precedence table: application-specific override, standard environment variable, specification fallback, and behavior when the user home cannot be resolved.
Clarify how unset and empty environment variables are interpreted, then implement that policy consistently.
Centralize path resolution in one function where practical instead of relying on scattered import-time constants.
Create nested destination directories recursively before writing, while preserving the repository's expected error handling.
Test each precedence-table row in an isolated process or with fixtures that fully restore environment and imported-module state.
Add edge cases for unset, empty, relative, and absolute environment values, unresolved home directories, and a missing parent hierarchy.
Search again for stale legacy paths and update user-facing documentation and help output.
Run focused tests, the broader configuration and persistence suites, and repository formatting or diff checks before concluding.
pitfalls: Do not treat focused test success as proof of correctness when the authoritative evaluation fails.
Mutating environment variables and reloading a module in-process can leak state or miss import-time behavior elsewhere.
Testing only the normal home-directory case can overlook missing-home, empty-variable, relative-path, and platform-specific behavior.
Changing a nested default path without recursive directory creation can break first-run persistence.
Documentation and implementation can drift if precedence rules are not expressed and tested as one matrix.
validation: Assert the application-specific override wins over the standard base-directory variable.
Assert the standard base-directory variable wins over the home-based fallback.
Assert the fallback matches the relevant specification when no overrides are set.
Verify a first write succeeds when no parent directories exist.
Run environment combinations in isolated processes to observe clean import-time resolution.
Confirm no old path remains in executable code, tests, help text, or documentation.
Run broader related suites because the evidenced focused tests and diff check still accompanied an authoritative failure.

excerpt.title: Encode opaque expression names as lookup keys, not AST identifiers
excerpt.scope: Applies to parsers that translate user-defined names or labels into a host-language AST for compilation or evaluation. The evidenced procedure represents arbitrary tokens as data keys accessed through one fixed, valid AST identifier rather than treating those tokens as host-language variable names. The targeted suite passed 82 tests, manual edge cases preserved token values, formatting checks passed, and [external outcome redacted].
steps: Locate where parser tokens become host-language identifier or name nodes.
Classify those tokens as language syntax or opaque user data; treat opaque names as data even when they resemble valid identifiers.
Replace direct identifier construction with a lookup expression that uses a fixed, valid internal name and stores the original token in a string or constant key node.
Bind the fixed internal name to an adapter or mapping in the evaluation environment.
Keep built-ins and unrelated globals unavailable when evaluating generated code.
Preserve the token text exactly when forwarding it to the matcher or resolver.
Exercise reserved constants, keywords, numeric-looking strings, punctuation-bearing names, and ordinary identifiers.
Run the focused parser/expression suite and repository consistency checks.

A narrow crash reproducer is insufficient validation; ordinary identifiers, operators, and grouping may regress.

Verify numeric-looking and punctuation-bearing tokens reach the matcher unchanged.
Verify ordinary names and existing boolean-expression behavior still work.

Run a whitespace or patch-integrity check; the evidenced change passed `git diff --check`.

excerpt.title: Validate case-insensitivity across the full parser pipeline
excerpt.scope: Use when a text format or command parser must accept case-insensitive keywords. The evidence shows that a regex-level change passed nine focused tests and formatting checks, but [external outcome redacted].
steps: Locate every stage that handles the keyword: lexical recognition, capture extraction, normalization, dispatch, validation, and semantic interpretation.
Choose one canonicalization boundary, such as converting recognized keywords to a standard case immediately after parsing, while preserving case-sensitive payload text.
Check all downstream equality tests, dictionary lookups, and branches for assumptions about original keyword casing.
Create a parameterized case matrix covering uppercase, lowercase, and mixed-case forms for each supported command family.
Exercise the public API using the exact default path from the report, as well as any explicit options used by existing tests.
Assert semantic results, including schema, values, and metadata, rather than merely asserting that parsing does not raise.
Add negative tests confirming that unrelated tokens and case-sensitive data remain rejected or preserved as intended.
Run the focused parser tests, the broader subsystem suite, and repository-required checks before concluding the change is complete.
If external evaluation still fails, treat the implementation as unverified and expand diagnostics rather than claiming the regex-level method is sufficient.
pitfalls: Treating one lowercase example and a focused test-file pass as proof that the complete behavior is correct.
Applying case-insensitivity only at recognition while leaving downstream comparisons, dispatch, or normalization case-sensitive.
Assuming a clean diff and passing nearby tests substitute for broader integration validation.
Inferring the external failure cause without diagnostic output from the evaluator.
validation: Run parameterized tests for upper-, lower-, and mixed-case variants of every command family.
Test through the documented public read API with default arguments.
Verify parsed structure and semantic values, not only successful recognition.
Run the complete relevant subsystem suite in addition to the modified test file.
Record the focused result separately from external evaluation; here, nine local tests passed but the official score was zero, so completeness was not established.

excerpt.title: Validate formatter metadata semantics before moving axis labels into legends
excerpt.scope: When a plotting or reporting layer converts axis ticks into standalone legend labels, preserve formatter metadata only after determining its semantics and intended placement. Identify all consumers that detach labels from their original axis context, such as legends, color guides, or summary tables.

Verify large-range guides preserve the actual numeric magnitude.

excerpt.title: Validate delegated database metadata across every schema path
excerpt.scope: Use when a derived, wrapper, or relationship field must preserve database-definition metadata from another field, such as collation, type modifiers, constraints, or other DDL-affecting parameters. The evidence supports inspecting canonical field parameters and generated SQL, but the failed evaluation shows that this must be paired with a focused regression test across the actual creation and alteration paths.
steps: Identify the source field that owns the database property and every derived field whose physical column must be compatible with it.
Trace all schema-generation entry points for both initial table creation and field alteration; record where each path obtains type and auxiliary database parameters.
Prefer deriving metadata from the source field's canonical database-parameter API instead of independently reconstructing values.
Check whether the framework intentionally filters, overrides, or transforms those parameters for relationship fields and backend-specific implementations.
Add a regression model containing a character primary or unique target with explicit metadata and at least one referencing field.
Assert the referencing column receives the metadata during initial schema creation.
Assert changing the target field causes both target and referencing columns to be altered compatibly before constraints are recreated.
Cover nullable and non-nullable references and any distinct relationship wrappers that share the implementation.
Run the narrow regression first, then the surrounding field and schema-editor suites, and inspect the final diff for unintended API or formatting changes.

Copying one metadata key at a wrapper or relation layer may be incomplete if creation, alteration, cloning, or backend-specific code obtains parameters through different paths.
A passing pre-existing schema test may exercise the target column but not the dependent column whose definition must remain compatible.
Do not claim the attempted implementation works when the authoritative evaluation failed.

Exercise initial creation and migration-based alteration separately.
Verify constraint creation succeeds after column alterations on a backend that enforces compatibility.
Run focused relationship-field tests plus the broader schema-editor suite.
Include a regression assertion on the dependent column itself rather than relying only on tests of the source field.
Treat any authoritative suite failure as evidence that coverage or propagation remains incomplete.

excerpt.title: Validate WAL recovery at both database and export layers
excerpt.scope: Applies to SQLite WAL recovery tasks that require exporting complete, ordered data. The passing evidence supports layered validation of the recovered database and final artifact; it does not establish which specific WAL-repair method caused the recovery.
steps: Recover or replay the WAL using an appropriate SQLite-compatible method while preserving the original files.
Query the recovered table and compare its row count with the task's expected total.
Verify required identifiers are present, unique, and ordered as specified.
Export records into the required serialization format using an explicit sort key.
Parse the exported artifact independently rather than trusting the export command's exit status.
Run SQLite integrity_check on the recovered database.
Confirm the parsed artifact's count and identifiers match the validated database query.
pitfalls: Treating a readable base database as complete when unapplied WAL records may exist.
Checking only the database or only the exported file; either layer can be correct while the other is incomplete.
Claiming a specific WAL-repair technique is proven when the evidence records only the successful result and validation.
validation: SQLite integrity_check returns ok.
The recovered table has the expected number of rows.
The output parses as valid JSON.
The JSON contains the expected number of records.
Identifiers are complete, unique, and sorted according to the requirement.
Database rows and exported records agree on key fields.
